lines.text: "The son of earth who struggles in the flaming sun and
fierily lashes the team of horses, who ardently wrestles to
reach a distant goal, covered in a cloud of dust—how could
he believe in the stars?'1
Such is the mysterious sway of the world that it presumes
to claim us wholly, so that we are cheated into thinking it
the ultimate reality; this is its uncanny tendency, to delude
us into thinking that it can satisfy us completely with its
gifts, can absorb us utterly with its duties. The consequence
is that the world itself becomes a god, rounded in itself,
closed and all-sufficient.
But if anyone sets his face against this claim made by the
world and refuses to become absorbed in its gifts or demands,
if anyone rejects the world's pretension to offer what is
finally decisive and important, then the world pursues him
with inexorable hatred. This hatred may take various forms:
it can assume the mask of seductive amiability, and it can
become open hostility and persecution. For if a man repudi-
ates the world's claim to have the power to fill his life
completely and utterly absorb his attention in the duties it
imposes, then it attempts to make clear to him that at any
rate it has the power to destroy him in infamy and torment.
These truths can be felt by anyone who still has an
awareness that all the care, all the passion in the world does
not in the last resort exhaust the potentiality of his being,
anyone who is still capable of not being stunned by clamour
and show, and in whom there still lives a nostalgic longing,
as it were, for the stars. This the poets also know. The poem
which we have just quoted about the fighter, the son of
earth, who in the struggles of noonday forgets the stars,
continues thus:
"Yet the team flags, the paths grow dark, the eternal stars
begin to glimmer, the majesty of inviolable law pervades the
gloom. The cries of battle cease. The day is judged."
